title: Infra: GPU Fleet Capacity, Cloud Networking, IaC Modules & CI/CD Guidelines
author: Alex Kim
content:
Overview

This team wiki page consolidates our current best practices for GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module conventions, and CI/CD/build recommendations for Redwood's inference infra. It is a living document intended to reduce onboarding friction and centralize operational decisions.

Goals

- Provide deterministic capacity planning guidance for hosted and dedicated GPU pools.
- Standardize Terraform modules and naming so teams can reuse secure primitives.
- Document CI/CD flows for infra modules and runtime images with safety gates.
- Offer concrete runbooks for common capacity incidents and planned scaling.

Scope

Covers: GPU fleet sizing and policies, cloud account organization (AWS-focused patterns), VPC & peering patterns for Private deployments, Terraform module conventions, GitHub Actions/CI pipelines, and runbooks for capacity incidents. Does not cover application-level autoscaling (see eng-platform docs) or model-level performance tuning (see eng-serving-runtime).

1) GPU Fleet & Capacity Planning

Summary

We operate three GPU pool types: HOSTED (multi-tenant, elastic), DEDICATED (reserved for enterprise customers), and PRIVATE (customer-managed VPCs). Each pool is tracked in the capacity dashboard (infra-gpu-capacity).

SLOs & Targets

- Median tail latency SLA for 512-token requests: HOSTED <= 250ms (p95 <= 400ms)
- DEDICATED throughput SLO: maintain 99% of committed QPS over a 30-day window
- Capacity provisioning lead time target: 72 hours for spot/elastic scaling, 14 days for reserved clusters

Key Metrics to Monitor

- GPU utilization (per-card and per-Attached-VM), target steady-state 55-70%
- Queue depth and per-route latency (p50/p95/p99)
- EViction/Preemption rate for spot-backed pools (<0.5% target)
- Time-to-allocate (provisioning latency) for new instances

Sizing Heuristics

- Baseline: start with 55% target utilization. Effective capacity = (cards * avg_tokens_per_sec_per_card * 0.55)
- Example: A80 cards running 8k-token/s equivalent provide baseline throughput T. For a 10k QPS target, assume model and batching profiles to compute required cards + 20% buffer for bursts.
- Reserve buffer: 15-25% headroom for rolling upgrades and regional failover.

Autoscaling & Policies

- Use continuous batching + request-based scaling for HOSTED pools. Scale-out triggers: sustained queue depth > 50 for 5m and average GPU util > 70% for 3m. Scale-in cool-down: 10m.
- DEDICATED pools use scheduled scale policies tied to commit windows plus manual override.

Ownership & Runbook Links

- Capacity owner: infra-sre@g.redwood.com
- Dashboard: infra-gpu-capacity (grafana)
- Immediate runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026

2) Cloud Accounts & Networking Patterns

Account Structure (AWS Recommended Pattern)

- Organization root: redwood-org
- Landing accounts: management, shared-services (logging/monitoring), security
- Workload accounts: prod-hosted, staging-hosted, prod-dedicated-us-west-2, private-onprem (customer-specific)

VPC & Network Design

- Use one VPC per region per workload account. Subnets: public (ingress LB), private (compute), db (private with no internet egress).
- Peering/Transit: prefer Transit Gateway for multi-account connectivity. For Private customer deployments, establish VPC peering or Transit Gateway attachments with customer-managed VPN/Direct Connect.

Egress & NAT

- Centralize egress through shared-services account: NAT gateways or egress VPC endpoints to apply egress filtering and egress logging.

Security & IAM Patterns

- Principle of least privilege: Terraform-managed IAM roles only. Use short-lived credentials (OIDC/IRSA) for pods and instance profiles for infra hosts.
- KMS: keys for each customer in private deployments; management keys in shared-services account.

3) Terraform / IaC Module Conventions

Module Layout

- repo: infra-modules (monorepo)
- top-level modules: vpc, batch-cluster, gpu-instance-profile, monitoring, iam

Conventions (required)

- Each module must have: README.md, examples/, variables.tf (with descriptions), outputs.tf, CHANGELOG.md
- Inputs: keep module inputs minimal and strongly typed. Avoid passing raw maps of unknown structure.
- Versioning: use semantic versioning tags (v1.2.0) and release with changelog. Modules used by customer infra must pin to a tag.

Example: gpu-instance-profile module inputs (table)

| input_name | type | description | default | required |
|------------|------|-------------|---------|----------|
| instance_type | string | EC2 instance type (e.g., p4d.24xlarge, g5.12xlarge) | \"p4d.24xlarge\" | yes |
| gpu_count | number | Number of GPUs per instance | \"1\" | yes |
| use_spot | bool | Use spot instances for lower cost | \"true\" | no |
| iam_role_name | string | Name of the instance profile role | \"\" | yes |

Module Security Checks

- All modules must pass terraform-compliance tests and terrascan policies in CI before merge.
- Sensitive outputs should never be exported; use SSM/KMS-backed secrets.

4) CI/CD & Build Pipelines

Principles

- Keep infra changes small and reviewable. Enforce plan reviews and automated checks.
- Separate pipelines for module development and environment deploy pipelines.

Pipeline Stages (recommended for infra-modules repo)

1. lint: terraform fmt + tflint
2. unit-checks: static security scanning (terrascan, checkov)
3. plan: terraform plan with -out and upload plan artifact to ephemeral storage
4. policy: run terraform-compliance / custom policies
5. integration: apply to ephemeral test account (auto-rollback on failure)
6. release: tag + publish module to module registry

Environment Deploy Pipelines (prod/staging)

- PR -> plan (comment with plan summary)
- Approvals: two approvers required for prod
- Apply strategy: automated apply for staging, gated apply for prod with Canary where possible

GitHub Actions Example Snippet

- name: Terraform Plan
  run: |
    terraform init -backend-config=\"bucket=${{ secrets.TERRAFORM_BUCKET }}\"
    terraform validate
    terraform plan -out=tfplan -input=false

Safety & Rollback

- Keep state backups and enable state locking (DynamoDB).
- When rolling a cluster, use canary node groups and drain traffic before termination.

5) Runbooks: Common Capacity Incidents

Incident: Sudden increase in queue depth / high p95 latency

1. Verify: check infra-gpu-capacity dashboard, p95 latency, and queue depth.
2. Check autoscaler: ensure scale-out jobs are not throttled and throttling metrics are healthy.
3. Mitigation (fast): increase desired capacity for HOSTED pools by +20% (console or infra control plane)
4. Mitigation (mid): enable burst pool (if configured) and route lower-priority tenants to reduced-QoS queue.
5. Post-incident: run retro, compute underprovision factor, and adjust policies.

Incident: GPU Preemption Spike (spot pools)

1. Verify preemption rate and impacted instances.
2. Migrate critical workloads to on-demand or reserved pools.
3. If on-demand not available, reduce batch sizes per-request to lower memory pressure and avoid OOMs.

Playbook: Emergency Capacity Expansion (72h timeline)

1. T-72h: submit capacity request ticket to cloud-ops with region, instance_type, estimated_cards_needed, and emergency contact.
2. T-48h: provision base instances and attach to test cluster. Run smoke tests (load test 10% of expected traffic).
3. T-24h: schedule DNS/vertica routing changes for cutover window; inform SRE and customer success.
4. T-0: perform rolling addition using canary nodes, validate telemetry, and promote nodes to service group.

6) Operational Playbook & Ownership

Alerting thresholds (examples)

- GPU util p95 > 85% for 10m -> P1 paged to infra-sre oncall
- Queue depth > 100 sustained 5m -> P1
- Preemption rate > 1% in spot pools for 10m -> P2

Owners

- infra-sre: capacity and alerts
- infra-platform: Terraform modules and CI pipelines
- infra-networking: VPC, peering, Transit Gateway

Oncall Runbook Links

- Primary runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- Incident postmortem template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortem-template

7) FAQ & Common Patterns

Q: When should a workload be moved from HOSTED to DEDICATED?
A: When an enterprise customer requires predictable throughput and isolation, or when committed throughput exceeds 5% of a single-region cluster capacity. See dedicated capacity sizing guidelines.

Q: How do I pick instance types?
A: Prefer A100/A800 or equivalent for model training and high-throughput inference. Use G5/G4 for cost-sensitive lower-memory models. Always reference benchmark profiles in eng-serving-runtime before finalizing.

Appendix: Useful CLI Commands

- Check cluster GPU utilization (kubectl + metrics):
  kubectl top nodes --selector=pool=gpu --use-protocol-buffers

- Trigger Terraform plan as a one-off (example):
  tfenv use 1.5.6
  terraform init -backend-config=\"bucket=redwood-terraform-state\"
  terraform plan -var='region=us-west-2' -out=tfplan

- Drain a GPU node (safe rolling update):
  kubectl cordon node/<node-name>
  kubectl drain node/<node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force

Maintenance & Next Steps

This doc should be reviewed quarterly and after any major incident affecting capacity or network topology. If you update module conventions or CI gates, notify infra-platform and add a changelog entry.

Feedback

Add comments to this page or open a PR against infra-team-wiki. For urgent changes, ping #infra-sre in Slack.
